slides.title: Purpose
bullets: A perianal swab is taken to find the eggs of E. vermicularis (pinworm).
The eggs are usually in the skin folds around the anus; sometimes a whole worm is seen in the stool.
Pinworm is common in children; if one child in a family is infected, other family members may be too.
The specimen is taken with sticky tape or with a swab wetted in saline; the swab method is described here. A swab can also collect Taenia eggs.

slides.title: Collecting the specimen
bullets: 1. You need cotton swabs, freshly made saline and a jar with about 5 mL of saline for the specimen.
2. To raise the chance of finding eggs, take the specimen in the morning before the patient goes to the toilet, or from the clothes worn overnight.
3. Wet the swab in saline and wipe the perianal area with it.
4. Rinse the swab in the jar of saline so that the eggs are washed off.

slides.title: Collecting the specimen
bullets: 5. Close the jar and dispose of the swab; label the jar with the patient’s name and the date and time of collection.

slides.title: Preparing the slide and microscopy
bullets: 1. Mark the request form, jar, test tube and slide with one number; pour the specimen in saline into the tube.
2. Balance the tubes and centrifuge for 1 minute so that the eggs settle.
3. Pour off the supernatant with a dropper; transfer the sediment to a slide with a bulb pipette.
4. Lower the cover glass, held by a corner, without air bubbles.

slides.title: Preparing the slide and microscopy
bullets: 5. Search for eggs with the 10× objective; close the condenser so there is not too much light, otherwise colourless eggs cannot be seen.
6. Identify the eggs with the 40× objective and record what is found.

slides.title: Reading the result
bullets: Normal: no helminth eggs found.
Pathology: E. vermicularis eggs found — the egg is smooth, with a colourless shell, oval with one side flattened, and contains a larva (which may look granular).
Female pinworms sometimes appear in the swab: they are white and small, and under a magnifying glass a long pointed tail may be seen.
E. vermicularis infestation rarely causes serious symptoms but may irritate the anal region considerably; in women it can affect the urogenital tract.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: A positive diagnosis may need several specimens taken on different days — one negative result does not exclude infestation.
To raise the chance of finding eggs, the specimen is taken in the morning before the toilet (or from the clothes worn overnight).
If the condenser is not closed enough, colourless eggs cannot be seen.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Perianal swabs may contain pathogenic organisms — parasites, bacteria and viruses; take the usual precautions.
By the time they reach the laboratory the eggs in many specimens may have become infective.
Wear single-use gloves; wash the hands after disposing of the swab and after work.
Balance the tubes in the centrifuge; do not open the lid until it has stopped completely.
Disinfect used jars and slides.

slides.title: Pinworm tape test (perianal sample)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Clear adhesive tape (or a sticky paddle) pressed on the perianal skin

What it is used for: The main sign of pinworm infection is itching around the anus, especially at night; many people have no symptoms. Some have trouble sleeping, restlessness or belly pain. According to CDC, the most common diagnostic test is the "tape test".

slides.title: Pinworm tape test (perianal sample)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Physiology: Female Enterobius vermicularis migrate out of the anus at night and lay eggs on the perianal skin. Eggs reach the mouth from scratching hands, under fingernails, and from contaminated clothes, bedding and objects, where they can survive 2–3 weeks if not cleaned. Infection is most common in school- and preschool-age children, people in institutions, and household members of an infected person.

slides.title: Pinworm tape test (perianal sample)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Under the microscope: eggs measure 50–60 × 20–30 µm, are transparent, elongate-oval and slightly flattened on one side, and are usually partly embryonated when laid. Adult females are 8–13 mm with a long pointed tail; males are up to 2.5 mm.

slides.title: Pinworm tape test (perianal sample)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 1/2
cols: Enterobiasis is confirmed when pinworm eggs are seen on the tape under a microscope, or adult worms are found in the perianal area or during anorectal or vaginal examination.
Treatment is prescribed by a doctor.
No eggs were seen on the tape. CDC advises doing the tape test three mornings in a row, so the results of all samples, not one, are considered together.

slides.title: Pinworm tape test (perianal sample)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result · 2/2
cols: CDC advises treating the infected person, caregivers and household members at the same time with two doses, the second two weeks after the first: the medicines kill worms but not eggs.

slides.title: Pinworm tape test (perianal sample)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: Sample first thing in the morning, before washing, using the toilet or dressing: press the sticky side of clear tape against the skin around the anus. Repeat three mornings in a row. Put the tape in a sealed container or zip bag; if a glass slide is provided, stick the tape onto its clear part. A commercial sticky "paddle" kit is an alternative — follow the maker's instructions.

Safety: do not touch your face while sampling, and wash hands thoroughly afterwards. In the laboratory, tape samples are handled with standard precautions to avoid swallowing infectious eggs; surfaces are cleaned thoroughly because the egg shell is sticky.

slides.title: Pinworm tape test (perianal sample)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Pinworm eggs are rarely found in stool; they are collected from the skin folds around the anus — especially in children. In the WHO method clear adhesive tape is stuck to a slide, looped over a spoon handle, pressed around the anus in several places and stuck back flat on the slide. Former-USSR textbooks also describe a swab scraping or wash; the sample is taken in the morning before washing or using the toilet and repeated several times.

Limitations: Stool, urine, vaginal or anorectal swabs usually do not contain enough eggs and are generally not collected; there is no blood test for pinworm. Eggs are occasionally found incidentally in stool, urine or cervical Pap smears.
